description: Jangada Orbital is a team from Fortaleza, Ceará, Brazil, taking on the Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge. We are a full-stack developer who works with telemetry and large datasets, two Telecommunications Engineering students from IFCE (one also at the Apple Developer Academy) and a Huawei ICT Academy hackathon veteran. Our goal: turn two decades of NASA fire data into one consistent fire calendar that emergency teams can trust. Team complete (3 members).
summary: MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) fire records cannot be compared directly: VIIRS detects about 6x more hotspots over Brazil. Jangada Orbital harmonizes both into one consistent monthly series and a burning activity calendar. Draw an area on the map to see which months and years burned most, whether this month is unusual versus the historical median, and download the data as CSV. Built on NASA FIRMS data for Brazil, 2000 to today.
details:
What it does. A web app for emergency responders, land managers and scientists, at https://matheus-c-feitosa.github.io/jangada-orbital/.

Areas:

- Brazil, the 27 states or the 6 IBGE biomes;

- any of the 5,570 municipalities, searched by name;

- a rectangle or polygon drawn on the map;

- a point and radius.

For the area, the app shows:

- Calendar. A month × year fire calendar from 2001 to today. Months above the 90th percentile of past years are flagged. The current, partial month is compared pro rata. Converted months show their likely range.

- Busiest periods. The busiest year, the highest month and the months that usually burn most.

- Yearly totals. The yearly totals with their conversion range, and this year so far against the normal band of past years.

- Fire season. When the season usually starts, peaks and ends, whether it is shifting, and how intense the fires are (fire radiative power and the share of night detections).

- Ranking. A ranking of states, biomes and municipalities by detections, by density per 1,000 km² or against their own normal, with a side-by-side comparison.

- Climate context. Optional El Niño and La Niña years (NOAA ONI).

- Maps. How many years each 0.1° cell burned; this year against normal by state or biome; and the near-real-time detections of the last 7 days.

- Downloads. The monthly series as CSV, and the calendar as a PNG image.

- Satellites. A switch between the harmonized series and the counts each satellite observed.

How it works.

1. A Python + DuckDB pipeline downloads the NASA FIRMS hotspots for Brazil: MODIS Terra and Aqua; VIIRS S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21. That is about 46 million hotspots in the yearly country files. It clips them to the official IBGE border. A cross-check against the FIRMS country files differs by −0.02%.

2. It keeps vegetation fires and collapses the VIIRS pixels of the same fire into ~1 km positions per overpass.

3. It counts hotspots per 0.1° cell and month.

4. VIIRS is calibrated to Aqua-MODIS-equivalent detections, with one factor per state and month of the year. The fit uses the years both sensors flew (2012–2020). Terra fills the first months before Aqua. From 2024 the series uses NOAA-20 and NOAA-21, put on the S-NPP scale.

5. Validation on held-out years (2021–2022) that the model never saw:

- 92% of national months and 96% of state-years land within ±20%, with a total bias of −2.2%;

- for state-months the error depends on the size of the month: 78% within ±20% when Aqua saw 500 or more detections, 62% over all state-months.

The first target (80% of all state-months) was not met. The Method page says so and shows the error by size.

6. The pipeline also builds the IBGE biome and municipality views, the recurrence grid, the ranking and the climate context.

7. The web app (React, TypeScript, MapLibre) is a static site on GitHub Pages:

- it reads pre-aggregated files, and the Parquet tiles of the 0.1° grid for drawn areas, directly in the browser;

- it has no server and needs no login;

- the first screen shows the answer in about 3 seconds on a 4G phone.

Benefits.

- A consistent 25-year fire history for any area of Brazil, where the sensor of origin no longer matters.

- It answers "is this month worse than usual?" and "when does the fire season come here?" in seconds.

- It is honest about what is estimated and how well.

Tools.

- Languages and libraries: Python, DuckDB, TypeScript, React, Vite, MapLibre GL, terra-draw, hyparquet, Tailwind CSS.

- Hosting: GitHub Pages.

- The code is under the Apache-2.0 license.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

We used Claude Code (Anthropic) as a coding assistant. It helped:

- research the challenge;

- plan the solution;

- write the data pipeline, the web app and the documentation.

Every SI-generated change was reviewed and tested by the team. Commits with SI-generated code carry a "Co-Authored-By: Claude" line, and docs/SI_USAGE.md logs what was generated and how we checked it.

The demo video is rendered by a script written with Claude Code: its title and end cards are drawn by code, and the app footage is screenshots of the live app. It carries a visible label, "Edited with SI-assisted code", for its whole length. The narration is a human voice, not SI-generated. The music bed is synthesized by a script written with Claude Code (SI-assisted audio, no samples). No SI-generated content uses NASA logos, flags or mission insignia.
dataRefs: NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System) active fire / hotspot data: MODIS Collection 6.1 (Terra, Aqua), 2000-today, and VIIRS 375 m (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21), 2012-today, from the yearly country archives and the FIRMS area API.
